name: Lebensraum
summary: Lebensraum (living space) is the doctrine that a nation's survival depends on holding enough land of its own to feed it, and that a growing people may therefore take territory by force. In Hitler's form it called for conquering Russia and the border states, settling them with Germans, and removing or subjecting the existing peoples, with rearmament, war and racial hierarchy as its means.
scope: The Nazi doctrine of eastward land conquest and German settlement as set out in Hitler's Mein Kampf (1925-26), the Second Book (1928), the 1937 Hossbach conference and his 1941-42 table talk, with its implementation in the eastern occupation plans. Positions are taken only where these texts and the scholarship on the doctrine state them; the wider Nazi programme on domestic politics, economy and society is not borrowed. The earlier geographers' overseas-colonial version (Ratzel) and later metaphorical uses are excluded.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Mein Kampf (Vol. 2, ch. 14) makes the acquisition of territory the objective of foreign policy and says the German sword must win the soil for the German plough; the Second Book and the 1937 Hossbach conference repeat that Germany's future depends on gaining space.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Mein Kampf (Vol. 1, ch. 1) says people of the same blood belong in one Reich, even where this is economically pointless, and that Germany may turn to acquiring foreign land only after bringing all Germans into one state; Hossbach names Austria and Czechoslovakia as the first targets.

population-transfer.rationale: The Hossbach conference counts on the compulsory emigration of 2 million people from Czechoslovakia and 1 million from Austria, and the eastern economic directives expected tens of millions in the occupied East to die or be pushed to Siberia.

majority-settlement.rationale: Hitler's table talk sets the aim of settling Germans in the conquered East (a hundred million in the long run, 'Germanise this country by the immigration of Germans'), regions where Slavs were the majority.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: The doctrine's whole aim is settlement of Germans on land held by the existing peoples of the East, with the natives treated as subject to German interests, so restricting outside settlement there is the opposite of its policy.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Hitler denies that any people holds land by a higher right (possession only shows the conqueror's strength) and tells his circle to treat the eastern natives as 'Redskins' to be displaced by German settlers.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Mein Kampf (Vol. 2, ch. 14) says no nation holds ground by a higher right, frontiers are chance products of struggle, and the right of possession lives only in strength; the claim rests on need and power, not on historical tie.

national-self-determination.rationale: The doctrine takes land from the Slavic peoples of the East and treats them as subjects or removable populations, so it cannot grant every nation the right to its own state; Mein Kampf says the national movement is the advocate of its own nation only, not 'a police guard for the poor small nations'.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The doctrine puts the conquered peoples of the East under German rule by force and for German interests ('we are not their overseers, all we are there for is to promote our own interests'), which is rule without their consent.

non-intervention.rationale: Conquest and annexation of other states' land by force is the doctrine's programme, as Mein Kampf and the Hossbach minutes state, so it denies that no state may interfere in another's affairs for any reason.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Mein Kampf says territory is obtained by the 'clenched hand' and the sword, not by the consent of others, and the doctrine's land policy ignores the wishes of the people living there.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Mein Kampf says possession of territory is established by the strength of the conqueror, and the doctrine plans annexation by force without regard to the inhabitants' consent.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Mein Kampf (Vol. 1, ch. 4; Vol. 2, ch. 14) says that when others refuse land 'the clenched hand must take by force', and that the German people must win territory by a triumphant sword; initiating war for land is the doctrine's method.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: The doctrine is a programme of wars of conquest: Mein Kampf says land must be won by the sword, and Hitler told his commanders in 1937 that Germany's problem could be solved only by force.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Mein Kampf calls pacifism nonsense, calls for all state power to be concentrated in land military forces and for the sword to win the soil, and the Second Book calls the army a necessary instrument.

arms-reduction.rationale: The doctrine needs armament well beyond what is needed for defence (Second Book, ch. 8, on the necessity of military power; Hossbach on completing rearmament for the war for space).

empower-police-military.rationale: Mein Kampf wants all means of power concentrated in the land forces, the Second Book stresses the necessity of military power, and Hossbach records rearmament as the precondition for gaining space; police are not addressed.

military-superiority.rationale: The Hossbach conference stresses striking while Germany's armament lead holds and before rivals catch up, and Mein Kampf says Germany must become a world power able to win land by arms.

conscription.rationale: Mein Kampf (Vol. 2, ch. 14) calls the abolition of compulsory national military service fatal for Germany and praises the Prussian army as the school of the national community.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The doctrine depends on soldiers fighting wars for land; Mein Kampf says 'we must be the soldiers of the German nation' and that the sword provides the soil.

war-builds-character.rationale: Mein Kampf (Vol. 1, ch. 4) says man has become great through perpetual struggle and that in perpetual peace his greatness must decline; the Second Book treats struggle as the precondition of evolution.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The Second Book (ch. 1) holds that the limits of living space compel a struggle for survival between peoples and that this struggle contains the precondition for evolution; Mein Kampf says the same.

nation-first.rationale: Mein Kampf (Vol. 2, ch. 14) says the national movement must be the protagonist of its own nation, not the advocate of others, and the Second Book defines foreign policy as fighting for the interests of the German people.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Mein Kampf calls hopes in the League of Nations a fantastic invention that diverts the Germans from real possibilities, and the Second Book says Germany's aims cannot be achieved through the League.

force-without-un.rationale: The Second Book says the measures to give Germany land must be carried out outside the League of Nations in Geneva; the UN is anachronistic here.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: The Second Book (ch. 10, 'No Neutrality') says no great state has risen by neutrality and that neutrality is weak surrender to a fate decided by foreign powers; Germany should ally with a power that serves its aim.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Mein Kampf and the Second Book call restoring the 1914 frontiers a glaring absurdity and not worth the blood, because the aim is new land in the East, not returned land.

limit-population.rationale: Mein Kampf (Vol. 1, ch. 4) rejects restricting the birth-rate as a solution, saying it robs the nation of its future, and holds that the answer to a growing population is more land.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Mein Kampf says a healthy peasant class of small and medium farmers is the basis of the national community and that the imbalance of town over country lies behind many present evils, and wants industry and commerce subordinate to it.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The doctrine fixes the nation on blood: Mein Kampf wants the German people to care for the purity of its blood and the eastern land to be settled by Germans, with the native population kept apart or removed.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Mein Kampf ranks peoples by race, calls the Germans the highest species and the peoples of the East racially inferior, and the Holocaust Encyclopedia describes the doctrine as resting on a racial hierarchy.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Mein Kampf mocks the 'sacred rights of man' as an objection to territorial expansion, and the doctrine's plans provide for the removal, enslavement or death of Slavs and Jews.

race-social-construct.rationale: Mein Kampf treats race as the real basis of humanity and attributes state-building ability to a Germanic race against 'races of inferior worth'.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Mein Kampf holds that peoples differ in ability by race, with Germanic peoples as the state-builders and the Slavs of 'inferior worth', and that this is a matter of blood.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The doctrine takes the struggle for land to be between racially defined peoples, each fighting for its own interest, and tells Germans to organise for the German people.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Mein Kampf (Vol. 2, ch. 14) says the Jews rule Russia and strive by Bolshevism for world dominion, and uses this to justify the eastern conquest.

defeat-communism.rationale: Mein Kampf says no alliance with Bolshevik Russia is possible, that Bolshevism cannot be tamed, and that the Jewish-led Russian state is ripe for dissolution by German conquest.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Mein Kampf calls for care for the purity of German blood, and Hitler wanted the German settlers' life kept as far apart as possible from the natives to prevent any fusion.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Hitler wanted German settlers' life kept apart from the natives, with separate pubs from which natives are excluded, and Himmler's memorandum (approved by Hitler) proposed racial screening of the eastern population and minimal schooling for the rest.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The Second Book criticises German colonial rule for acting as teacher of the natives, and Hitler said Russians and Ukrainians should be given no schooling beyond road signs, since the Germans were there only to promote their own interests.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Mein Kampf and the Second Book say the victor powers, France above all, aim to dismember and weaken Germany.

state-harmful.rationale: The doctrine is carried out by state power: Mein Kampf says the army and the state organise the winning of land and the Prussian state idea is a lasting success; a stateless view contradicts it.

missingStatements.text: A nation that lacks enough land to feed its people may take land from other peoples by war.
missingStatements.rationale: Mein Kampf says the clenched hand must take by force what the open hand of friendship is refused, since the soil must be won by a triumphant sword.

missingStatements.text: The native inhabitants of a conquered region may be cleared out and replaced by settlers from the conquering nation.
missingStatements.rationale: Hitler aimed to settle a hundred million Germans in the East, and the 1941 economic directives expected tens of millions of locals to die or be moved to Siberia.

missingStatements.text: A people should feed itself from its own territory rather than depend on international trade.
missingStatements.rationale: The Second Book calls it sick and dangerous for a people to rely on international trade and industry, and says a healthy people satisfies its needs from its own land.

notes:
Themes searched in the full texts of Mein Kampf, the Second Book, the Hossbach minutes and the table talk: economy, government, society, world, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, means, globalism. The doctrine is about land, war, race and settlement, so economy, government, liberty and technology are mostly null. The 1920 NSDAP programme (point 3) asks for land and territory 'colonies' while Mein Kampf, the Second Book and Hossbach reject overseas colonial policy for European land, so colonies-serve-metropole is null: none of them says how overseas territories should be governed. Britannica's article was blocked (Cloudflare). Many answers rest on a stated opposite (a statement that the doctrine's land policy contradicts), as rules 3 allow.
